intro: Stockholm's City Hall took twelve years to build, eight million bricks, and one deliberate provocation: its tower stands exactly one meter taller than Copenhagen's. Every December the world watches the Nobel Banquet in its Blue Hall.
page_title: Stockholm City Hall: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Architect Ragnar Ostberg won the City Hall commission in 1903 and spent the next two decades refining it. Construction ran from 1911 to 1923 on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen island, facing Riddarfjarden. Ostberg designed in the National Romantic style, a deliberate turn away from continental classicism toward Swedish brick, craft traditions, and medieval references. The building rose as a small city in itself: offices and council chambers for Stockholm's government wrapped around two courtyards, the Blue Hall and the Borgargarden, the citizens' courtyard. It was inaugurated on 23 June 1923, the 400th anniversary of Gustav Vasa's entry into Stockholm. And the tower, at 106 meters, was built exactly one meter taller than the tower of Copenhagen City Hall. In the early 1900s, that kind of thing still mattered.
sections.heading: Twelve years of brick

sections.body: The Stadshustornet, the City Hall Tower, is the building's exclamation mark. Its shaft took almost 2.5 million bricks and weighs 24,000 tonnes, double the Eiffel Tower. Inside, 365 steps climb past the Tower Museum to the viewpoint 73 meters above sea level, guarded by four sculptures including Eric IX, Stockholm's patron saint. The belfry holds nine bells, the largest 3,000 kg, striking every hour with tunes at noon and 6 pm. When the tune plays, figures emerge on the eastern balcony and turn through the story of St. George and the Dragon. Above it all stand the Three Crowns, Tre Kronor, Sweden's national emblem since the 14th century: gilded copper, each 2.2 meters wide and 70 kg, angled toward Gamla Stan, where the medieval Tre Kronor castle stood until it burned in 1697. Ostberg was echoing that lost spire on purpose.
sections.heading: The tower and the crowns

sections.body: The Blue Hall was supposed to be blue. Ostberg planned plastered walls in the hall's namesake color, but as the red brick rose he fell in love with it and ordered the plastering stopped. The name stuck anyway. Since 1934 the hall's building has hosted the Nobel Banquet every 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death: first in the Golden Hall, and in the Blue Hall itself in 1950 and every year from 1974 on. It is a white-tie dinner for over a thousand guests, broadcast live on Swedish television with the kind of ratings and commentary usually reserved for the Olympics. After dinner the party moves upstairs to the Golden Hall for the dance, among 18 million gold mosaic pieces depicting Swedish history, dominated by the great mosaic of the Queen of Lake Malaren. The Council Chamber, where Stockholm's council meets, got a ceiling built like a Viking longhouse. A documentary for the 2023 centenary, Medborgarnas palats (The Citizens' Palace), told the building's story through strikes, war, and the craftsmen who built Sweden's last great hand-made monument.
sections.heading: The Blue Hall that stayed red

sections.body:
The Nobel Banquet is Sweden's biggest annual television event after the fact: held every 10 December in the Blue Hall and broadcast live on SVT with high ratings, it turns the City Hall into the most televised building in Sweden for one night a year. Newspapers print seating diagrams of the table of honor, commentators dissect gowns and flower arrangements like Olympic coverage, and the whole country watches royalty and laureates dine where the brick was never painted blue.

The building's centenary brought its own film. Medborgarnas palats (2023) documented Ostberg's fight through strikes, war and crisis to raise the last monumental building in Sweden built entirely by hand, with archive material from the construction years and access to the tower, the halls and the workshops behind the Nobel glamour.
